sum: Canadian e-commerce platform Shopify (SHOP) reported third-quarter results with profit beating expectations, but two core growth metrics that investors were watching closely—platform gross merchandise volume (GMV) and subscription revenue—both fell short of market consensus. Combined with a decline in gross margin, disappointed selling pressure emerged on the third, sending the stock down 8.74% to close at $142.57, bringing its year-to-date decline to more than 11%.

Shopify's third-quarter revenue rose 32% year over year to $3.742 billion (about NT$120 billion), slightly below analysts' estimate of $3.75 billion. Adjusted earnings per share climbed to $0.49 from $0.34 a year earlier, beating the market expectation of $0.46. What really moved the stock was GMV: the metric measuring platform transaction activity reached $119.145 billion (about NT$3.9 trillion) in the third quarter, up 29% year over year, below the market consensus range of $119.9 billion to $120.1 billion, with growth also slowing markedly from 31% in the prior quarter.

Subscription solutions revenue also missed expectations, coming in at $836 million (about NT$27 billion) in the third quarter, up 20% year over year but below analysts' estimates of $848 million to $850 million. Subscription gross profit was $661 million (about NT$22 billion), also below the expected $680 million.

Some institutions had bet on more optimistic growth rates ahead of the report. Morgan Stanley had originally estimated GMV growth of about 33% and gross profit growth of 31% to 32%, according to reports; actual results showed GMV growth of about 29.5% and gross profit growth of 28%, and the shortfall became the main reason for the stock's pressure.

Looking at the revenue mix, Shopify's growth momentum remains concentrated in businesses tied to merchant transactions. Merchant solutions revenue reached $2.906 billion (about NT$95 billion) in the third quarter, up 35% year over year and accounting for about 78% of total revenue. Within that, transaction volume processed by its own payments and digital wallet platform Shopify Payments reached $81.4 billion (about NT$2.7 trillion), up 35% year over year, with payment penetration rising from 65% to 68%.

Shopify Shares Tumble as Q3 GMV and Subscription Revenue Miss; Holiday Guidance Draws Scrutiny
sum: Shopify Inc. (SHOP) shares fell sharply in premarket trading Tuesday after the Canadian e-commerce platform posted third-quarter results that beat on profit but came in light on the metrics investors track most closely: gross merchandise volume and subscription revenue.

The stock was down roughly 9% in early trading and had dropped as much as 19% in the premarket session, according to several market reports. The selloff came even though revenue grew 32% year over year to $3.74 billion and adjusted earnings of 49 cents a share topped the 46-cent consensus.

At the center of the disappointment was GMV, the total value of goods sold through Shopify's platform. It rose about 30% to $119.15 billion from $92.01 billion a year earlier, but analysts had been looking for roughly $120 billion, according to StreetAccount. Subscription revenue climbed 20% to $836 million, short of the $848.1 million FactSet estimate, while subscription gross profit of $661 million missed the $680.3 million consensus by nearly $20 million.

Merchant Solutions, the larger of Shopify's two revenue streams, outperformed. Revenue there rose 35% to $2.91 billion, slightly ahead of the roughly $2.9 billion estimate, and merchant gross profit also beat.
"We extended our track record of consistent execution, with 32% revenue growth and a 22% free cash flow margin," Chief Financial Officer Jeff Hoffmeister said in the company's release.

Profitability metrics were a bright spot. Gross profit increased 28% to $1.78 billion, operating income jumped 66% to $568 million from $343 million, and net income rose to $462 million from $264 million. Adjusted net income, excluding equity investments, climbed to $584 million from $367 million.

Free cash flow reached $816 million, up from $507 million a year earlier, lifting the margin to 22% from 18%. Operating expenses of $1.21 billion came in below the $1.26 billion analysts expected, helping operating income clear the $523.9 million consensus. Monthly recurring revenue rose 19% to $230 million, roughly in line with estimates.

Canada Just Finalized a Digital Trade Deal With Europe: Shopify Stock Could Be a Quiet Winner
sum: A small business can find a customer overseas in seconds and still face a much longer job completing the sale. Data rules, consumer protections, and the practical work of selling across borders all enter the picture. Canada and Europe’s digital trade announcement could make that environment more predictable.

The Canada-EU summit concluded substantive negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement intended to complement the Canada-Europe Trade Agreement (CETA). It isn’t an agreement already operating in full. The promised benefits include greater legal certainty and easier cross-border data flows, with implementation still ahead. That distinction prevents an encouraging policy development from becoming a speculative boost to this quarter’s company earnings.

For a merchant, predictability can help when choosing a market, a service provider, or a way to manage customer information. It doesn’t remove shipping bills, sales taxes, or every local requirement. The commercial gain comes when fewer obstacles make an additional sale worthwhile. More workable markets give a successful merchant somewhere else to grow.

The alliance also reaches beyond shopping websites to digital infrastructure and trust. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s summit reminder that the framework needs to be filled “with life now” fits online trade particularly well. Governments can set clearer rules, while businesses still need customers willing to spend. Shareholders earn from that activity, not the size of a signing ceremony.

Shopify (TSX: SHOP) supplies the tools merchants use to run stores, take payments, and manage commerce across channels. Its business increasingly earns from merchant activity alongside subscriptions. That’s an appealing link to easier trade because an existing customer can use more services as sales expand, without Shopify needing to become the seller of the goods itself.

Second-quarter revenue rose 34% to about US$3.6 billion. Merchant-solutions revenue increased 37%, faster than subscriptions. These services connect Shopify to transactions and other merchant needs. The growth shows that the company’s opportunity extends beyond adding another monthly software subscriber. It can earn more as the activity moving through its platform becomes larger.

sum: A pair of bullish analyst revisions and fresh data pointing to accelerating U.S. online spending have pushed Shopify shares to within a hair of their 52-week peak, with investors now positioning for the company's third-quarter report early next month.

The stock changed hands at EUR 159.88 in European trading, just 1.1% below its 52-week high of EUR 161.66. The advance follows a 2.7% gain on Thursday, when the shares closed at EUR 158.86, driven largely by a wave of price-target increases on Wall Street rather than any single company-specific catalyst.

Stifel lifted its target on Shopify from $180 to $210 on Wednesday while keeping a buy rating, citing sustained growth expectations for the platform. Baird followed the same day, raising its target from $160 to $190 and maintaining an Outperform rating after reviewing its own quarterly data and industry checks.

RBC analyst Paul Treiber added his voice on Friday, reaffirming an Outperform rating and nudging his target from $180 to $200. Treiber's case rests on hard sector numbers: U.S. e-commerce revenue climbed 8.2% year over year in August and September, up from 7.4% growth in the April-to-May stretch.

That momentum feeds directly into RBC's gross merchandise volume forecast. The firm now expects Shopify's third-quarter GMV to rise roughly 32.3% to $121.8 billion, well above the consensus estimate of a 30.3% gain to $119.9 billion.
The projections extend a brisk run for the platform. In the second quarter of 2026, Shopify grew revenue 34% to $3.58 billion while generating $654 million in free cash flow.

Management is simultaneously widening the company's payments and commerce infrastructure. According to media reports, Shopify plans to roll out its Shop Pay checkout service in India by the first quarter of 2027, with early talks already underway with local payment providers — a move that would open the door to one of the world's fastest-growing digital markets.

Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt said the selloff linked to Meta Pay’s appearance on Muse was not justified, adding that Meta Pay is an extension of Meta’s existing wallet rather than a new threat to Shopify Payments.
At the time of writing, SHOP shares were trading around 3% lower.

Rosenblatt contacted Muse to understand the addition of Meta Pay, according to TheFly. Muse said Meta Pay is Meta’s own wallet, the same one used for payments on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. It said customers who have saved a card for a Facebook Marketplace purchase or an Instagram shop can use those saved cards when making a purchase through Muse.
Muse also said it cannot see card numbers, with the payment information remaining in the user’s Meta Accounts Center, where the feature can be managed or disconnected.
Rosenblatt concluded that Meta Pay “does not seem to be disruptive to Shopify Payments or Shop Pay in its current form” and therefore does not view the more than 7% decline as warranted.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week that Meta and Shopify plan to let Muse place orders at Shopify-powered stores. Checkout is meant to run through Shop Pay, Shopify’s saved-details, one-tap payment tool. CEO Tobias Lütke said on X that the aim is an “easy and delightful way to shop and check out with Muse.”

sum: Shopify Inc. (NASDAQ: SHOP) shares jumped 11.6% on Monday, closing at $179.14, in one of the stock’s strongest single-day performances of the year.
The rally came despite a lackluster broader market, with the Nasdaq slipping and the S&P 500 roughly flat, underscoring that the move was largely stock- and sector-specific.
The primary catalyst was a bullish research note from RBC Capital, which introduced a new “total cost of ownership” framework to assess software companies’ vulnerability to AI-driven disruption.

Evaluating 14 major software firms — including Salesforce, Microsoft, and Adobe — RBC concluded that Shopify possesses “great defensibility” against AI-native competitors, a finding that directly countered a bearish thesis that had battered the stock the prior week.

That earlier sell-off stemmed from a July 21 downgrade by Rothschild & Co Redburn, which cut Shopify to Neutral, warning that Meta’s push into AI-powered small-business commerce tools posed an “existential threat” to roughly half of Shopify’s U.S. business. Shares had declined sharply in the days that followed before Monday’s sharp rebound.

Monday’s gains were amplified by sector-wide enthusiasm — rival Wix.com also surged more than 10% — alongside a risk-on market backdrop driven by easing geopolitical tensions, falling oil prices, and lower Treasury yields, conditions that typically favor high-multiple growth stocks.

Investors are also positioning ahead of Shopify’s second-quarter earnings report, due before market open on August 5, with consensus estimates near $3.44 billion in revenue. Analysts will be watching payments penetration, margins, and transaction losses closely as key indicators of the company’s underlying health.

Shopify (SHOP) lost one of its most committed bulls on July 21, and the note explaining why is unusually blunt about what changed.

Rothschild & Co Redburn analyst Dominic Ball downgraded Shopify to Neutral from Buy and cut his price target to $130 from $160, citing what he called an “existential threat” from AI and pointing specifically at Meta Platforms. Ball expects Meta to give small businesses AI tools to build storefronts, run ads, handle payments, and manage customer relationships, all of which Shopify sells today. “With a heavy heart, we downgrade Shopify to Neutral. It has been one of our highest conviction internet names,” he wrote, adding that “the downgrade is predominantly due to the Meta threat.” He estimates 50% of Shopify’s U.S. business is exposed.

Shares gapped lower at the open on July 21 before recovering much of the decline. By late morning, Shopify traded at $123.06, down 1.14%, while the Nasdaq gained 1.58%. The stock then closed at $118.42 on July 22, down $4.61 or 3.75%, according to TIKR data.

On the Q1 2026 call, Ball asked whether AI was accelerating small merchant sign-ups and whether integrations with tools like Claude and ChatGPT risked pushing Shopify back from the merchant’s user experience.

President Harley Finkelstein answered the second half without hedging: “Agents do not bypass Shopify, just the opposite. In fact, they write right into Shopify.” He pointed to ChatGPT moving to in-app browsers at checkout, meaning the buyer sees a Shopify storefront inside the chat window, with the economics unchanged.

Ball has now downgraded the risk that the answer was meant to close. He did not reference the call in his note and cited Meta as his reason, so this is a contrast between two documented positions rather than a stated cause.

This was a valuation call from a skeptic, not an AI endorsement.
